pairs.en: *“Rejoicing, I shall sing of your falling asleep.”* (Irmos, Ode 1)

sections.heading: Why the Church sings at this grave: death has become a sleep

pairs.en: Brethren, what does it mean that the Church calls the end of the Mother of God not death, as we ordinarily call the end of a human life, but a falling asleep — which is to say a repose, a peaceful sleep — and that she not only does not grieve or weep at her tomb, but on the contrary sings joyful, triumphant hymns at her departure? It means that the most blessed Mother of the Lord did not in fact die as people ordinarily die, but as it were fell asleep for a little while in a peaceful sleep after the heavy sorrows of her life; and that her tomb, which was for her a door to the heavenly kingdom, holds within it much joy for the Christian. From this tomb, as from the tomb of the risen Lord, heavenly incorruption breathes upon us also; or better to say, this tomb unfailingly promises us too immortality of soul and incorruption of body, destroying in us the fear of death. Glory to the Conqueror of death, the Lord Jesus! Before His coming, death was very terrible for man, because it carried off its prey beyond recall, and there was no means whatever of escaping it, since sin, in which death had its strength, poured itself out like a flood of the sea, and nothing had the power to stop that flood; and meanwhile it was known that those whom death had carried off were held as prisoners in the place to which people ordinarily departed after death. There were, it is true, two or three examples: two men who never experienced death at all, and one who by prayer and tears obtained a reprieve from death at the very moment when it had already raised its murderous hand over him, and it was forbidden to touch him for another fifteen years. But what did these two or three examples mean beside the millions of people who died? The same as a drop in the ocean. Besides, the last example was not altogether comforting for people, because King Hezekiah could not, after all, free himself from death entirely, but only prayed himself a reprieve from it; and the first two — Enoch and Elijah — were considered inimitable in the holiness of their lives, for which they were taken up to heaven alive. What do we see now, after the appearing of the Lord in our flesh and after the victory He won over sin and death? All the horror of death has vanished; it has become like a peaceful sleep, after which will dawn the joyful morning of the universal resurrection. In the measure that each of us conquers the sin that still lives in us — and now every means of conquering it has been given us (2 Peter 1:3) — the fear of death vanishes too, so that the triumphant conquerors of sin meet the bed of death with joy, and no longer die, but simply fall asleep in a peaceful sleep. “Now,” says St Chrysostom, “the Lord has crushed the gates of hell and destroyed the very face of death. But what am I saying — the face of death? He has changed the very name of death: for it is now called no longer death, but repose and sleep.” The clearest example of triumph over death we see in the most pure Mother of the Lord. She lay down in the tomb only for a brief rest of the flesh. We say brief because, by the witness of tradition, on the third day after her death her most pure body was no longer found in the tomb; it had been raised and taken up to heaven, where, together with her soul, it began to delight in heavenly blessedness. After the Mother of God we see the apostles and the martyrs, who meet death with joy, as the greatest of friends, who in exchange for the fast-fading goods of this present world — or in exchange for its troubles and sorrows — bestows on them the eternal joys of the Kingdom of heaven. After them we see all the saints, who likewise looked upon death with joy, seeing in it the end of earthly labours and the beginning of heavenly glory. Holy Church strives to plant the same fearlessness toward death in us as well, urging us to drive out the fear of it by gradually uprooting the sins within us; and she now calls her dead nothing other than “the departed who have fallen asleep” — as though they were only sleeping — because immortal life in the age to come is now so certain for us, and our right to it so sure, that we cannot, and must not, look upon death as anything but sleep. Glory to the infinitely good God! Formerly people wept long and inconsolably over the dead, and it was even expressly commanded to shed tears over them: “My son,” says the divinely enlightened sage, “let your tears fall over the dead, and begin lamentation as one who suffers grievously... Make bitter weeping and fervent wailing, and observe mourning as he deserves” (Sirach 38:16–17). But now, in place of funeral lamentation, we sing the hymn Alleluia — that is, “praise God” — extolling the divine wisdom and goodness which has made death a passage to immortality.

sections.heading: The icon of the Dormition: learn to make death a peaceful sleep

pairs.en: Brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling! You have seen on the icon of the all-honourable and glorious Dormition of the Mother of God how peacefully she reposes: what calm, what a reflection of heavenly joy upon her face! It is truly a sleep, a brief passage from earth to heaven. Let us too, then, learn by zeal for virtue and contempt for vice to make our own death a peaceful sleep. For as long as sin reigns in us, so long will death also be terrible for us, because truly, *“the death of sinners is evil.”* (Psalm 33:22) Sin is the cause of death: *“the wages of sin,”* it is said, *“is death.”* (Romans 6:23)

sections.heading: Conquer sin: hard at first, then easy and sweet

pairs.en: Let us then conquer sin in ourselves as far as our strength allows, for it is the cause of death. Conquering it is very hard only at the beginning; afterwards it becomes both easy and sweet, for as the sufferings caused by the struggle with sin increase, the consolation of Christ (2 Corinthians 1:5) will increase in us as well; and the Lord, who said that His yoke is good and His burden light (Matthew 11:30), will surely make the labours of those who strive light and life-giving too. Besides, what is won by labour is prized more dearly, and we take the greater delight in it. We were created for labour, not for softness and idleness. Yes, heavenly glory, which has no end, is beyond all doubt worth the labours, such as we can manage, of a whole lifetime. That incomparable blessedness, that kingdom of glory, is not given for nothing. *“The kingdom of heaven,”* it is said, *“suffers violence”* — that is, it is won by force — *“and the violent take it by force.”* (Matthew 11:12)

sections.heading: Weak faith in the age to come is why we are slothful

pairs.en: Is it not because our faith in the life of the age to come is weak that we are so slothful in conquering the passions and evil inclinations within us? Yet that life is as certain as this present life of ours. Will He who gave us the beginning of life here on earth not give us full, perfect life in heaven? Yes, this must inevitably be; indeed it is harder for it not to be than to be. And of this the unerring word of God assures us: *“all who are in the graves,”* it says, *“shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and having heard shall live, and shall come forth — those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.”* (John 5:28–29)

sections.heading: Stand ready at the border between two lives

pairs.en: Brethren! Eternal life beyond the grave is subject to no doubt whatever. But it is equally beyond the least doubt that it can be of two kinds: for the righteous, blessed; for hardened sinners, full of torment. Death is the boundary, the border between the present life and the life to come, and we do not know whether it lies far from us or near. Let us be ready at every moment to stand upon that dread border between the two lives. Amen.
